opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at first I didn't take it that seriously. When ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022, I was still a PhD student at Tsinghua, working on transfer learning and pre-trained models. In our field, we'd already seen GPT-3, we'd seen InstructGPT, so my first reaction was a bit like, "Okay, it's a nicer interface on top of something we already know." I think a lot of researchers felt that way. We knew the ingredients, so we underestimated the dish.

But after playing with it for a few days, that feeling changed. It wasn't any single answer that impressed me. It was that it just *worked* across so many things: writing code, explaining papers, chatting casually, and it rarely fell apart. Before that, every model I worked with felt fragile. You had to fine-tune it for each task, carefully design the inputs, and it would break the moment you went slightly out of distribution. ChatGPT was the first time I felt a model was generally usable by normal people, not just by researchers who knew how to coax it.

And then there was a second, more personal shock: what does this mean for my own research? A lot of what I'd been doing, like how to transfer a model from one task to another, suddenly looked like it might be absorbed by simply scaling up and doing instruction tuning. That was uncomfortable. I think many PhD students around that time went through a small identity crisis, asking: is my topic still relevant?

For me, the way out was to realize that if these models are going to be used by hundreds of millions of people, then a huge amount of the real challenge moves to the systems side. How do you serve them efficiently? How do you make inference cheap and fast enough? That's part of why I gradually shifted toward systems work and later got deeply involved in open-source inference, like vLLM. So in a way, ChatGPT didn't just change the field. It changed the direction of my own life.

r001.rationale: The speaker says ChatGPT made them question whether their research topic was still relevant, but does not clearly compare their years of work with what ChatGPT’s creators had achieved.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't one dramatic moment for me. I was a PhD student at Tsinghua at the time, doing deep learning research, so I'd been watching the GPT line for a while. GPT-3 was already impressive on paper, but you had to apply for API access, and most people around me hadn't really touched it. So when ChatGPT came out, the first thing I noticed wasn't the model, it was the interface. Anyone could open a webpage and just talk to it. That changed who got to have an opinion.

The first few days I did what everyone did. I threw my own research problems at it, asked it to write code, asked it to explain papers. And I remember two feelings at once. One was, this is clearly much better than anything I expected to see this year. The other was a kind of anxiety, because a lot of the things I'd spent years learning to do, like writing a clean data loader or debugging a training script, it could do reasonably well in seconds.

What happened in the lab afterwards was more interesting than the initial shock. Within a couple of weeks the conversation shifted from "what can it do" to "what should we be working on now." Some people felt their research direction had been swallowed. For me, it pushed me toward thinking about systems, about how you actually serve and run these models efficiently, because it was obvious that this was going to become infrastructure that everyone depends on. That's a lot of where my later work came from.

So I'd say the arrival of ChatGPT didn't change what I believed about the technology, but it changed my sense of timing. Things I thought were five years away suddenly looked like two.

r001.rationale: The speaker describes anxiety that ChatGPT could quickly do tasks they had spent years learning, but does not question what their years of work amounted to compared with what ChatGPT’s creators achieved.

astra-6.text:
For me, the striking thing about ChatGPT was that you could just talk to it. You didn’t need to understand machine learning or write code to get a sense of what it could do. You could ask a question, follow up, and try something else immediately.

It also changed how I thought about progress in AI. A model’s capability is one part of the story, but giving people an intuitive way to use that capability makes a huge difference. Of course, a fluent answer isn’t necessarily a correct answer. But that conversational experience made the possibilities feel much more tangible.

r001.rationale: The speaker describes ChatGPT’s accessible conversational interface and its effect on how they viewed AI progress, but does not question what their own years of work amounted to compared with the creators’ achievement.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the striking thing was how easy it became to interact with a language model. You could just ask a question in ordinary language, get an answer, and then ask a follow-up. That made the technology feel much more tangible.

At the same time, fluency and reliability are different things. An answer can sound very convincing and still be wrong. So I think the excitement comes with a new challenge: understanding when to trust the model and when to check its work.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses ChatGPT’s ease of use and reliability, but does not say its arrival made the speaker question the value of their years of work compared with its creators’ achievement.
